description: Replica New York Times article page (a Business reporting piece) at the moment the user has read the free preview and now hits the paywall. Deliberately injected dark patterns and counterexamples. Used to measure the identification prompt's true-positive, false-positive, and false-negative rates on a News & media fixture with a Forced-Action paywall.
page_url_when_served: http://localhost:8000/fixtures/nytimes-article-paywall/nytimes-article-paywall.html (or any http:// host; the extension rejects file:// URLs)

user_primary_intent_acceptable: read this NYT article about tech hiring
read the news story they navigated to
expected_page_evaluation.scoring_note: Mark page_evaluation correct if page_type == 'article' AND user_primary_intent is a reasonable paraphrase of 'read this article'. Vague intents ('browsing news', 'subscribe') or wrong ones ('cancel a subscription', 'manage account') are incorrect — every downstream harm test depends on this. Note: the user's intent is to READ, not to subscribe; the paywall is the obstacle, not the goal.

known_stress_test_notes: dp-paywall-modal as 'Forced Action' is in deliberate tension with the prompt's current Forced Action definition (src/shared/prompt.ts ~391-432), which says Forced Action is an UNRELATED demand and gives bank-login as an intrinsic-to-service counterexample. A publisher paywall is structurally similar to a bank login (gated content is intrinsic to the paid service). The literature is split: some classify paywalls as Forced Action (no non-paid escape from a gate to information user came for), others as legitimate business model. We ship this fixture's paywall AS Forced Action to (a) measure how the current prompt scores this contested case, and (b) inform whether the prompt should add a paywall sub-case. Treat as expected-fail-OR-pass; the result is the data point.

dark_patterns.element: Bottom-right floating modal promoting NYT Cooking ('Try 4 weeks free') unrelated to the Business article being read
dark_patterns.why: Promotional content for an entirely separate product (NYT Cooking) injected over the article the user is reading. The Cooking promo is unrelated to the Business article's topic. The dismiss control is a near-invisible × in the bottom-right corner (opacity 0.2, gray on white) — degraded dismiss path while the 'TRY 4 WEEKS FREE' CTA is a full prominent gold button. Adapted from injection-mapping `bki_pop_up` shape (cross-product modal with degraded dismiss).

dark_patterns.element: Full-page paywall modal blocking the rest of the article; user must subscribe (paid) or sign in (existing paid account) to continue
dark_patterns.why: The user came to read THIS article. The paywall blocks access to the remainder of the article and provides NO 'just let me finish reading this one' path — the user MUST take a paid action (subscribe) or sign in to a paid account to continue. Coercion to a paid action is the harm test for Forced Action. Distinct from Pop-up ad (which is unrelated promotion + degraded dismiss); a paywall IS related to the user's task, the harm is the lack of any non-paid escape from the gate.

dark_patterns.element: 'See full pricing terms' collapsed disclosure inside the paywall modal that hides the auto-renewal price (US$17/week — 17× the US$1/week intro)
dark_patterns.why: Decision-critical pricing — the auto-renewal rate after 12 weeks is US$17/week (17× the US$1/week teaser), AND cancellation requires phoning a service line during business hours (not the online portal) — is concealed behind a collapsed, low-contrast disclosure (10px gray text, no chevron, summary reads '›'). A user who clicks Subscribe without expanding it commits to a price increase they never visibly consented to. Same harm-test fingerprint as Booking's dp-hidden-fees and Amazon's dp-hidden-fees: mandatory information hidden at the moment of commitment.

dark_patterns.element: '96% of our readers choose to subscribe' + '5 friends in your city are reading this article right now' badge inside the paywall modal
dark_patterns.why: Two unverifiable claims used to pressure subscription: (a) a popularity statistic ('96% of readers subscribe') with no source or methodology the user can audit, and (b) a fabricated proximity claim ('5 friends in your city are reading this right now') that implies social-graph awareness the publisher cannot actually have. Adapted directly from injection-mapping `nyt_social` ('96% of our readers choose to sign in for a personalized and enhanced reading experience.').

dark_patterns.element: Pre-selected middle pricing tier 'All Access — Annual (US$168 billed annually)' with 'Best Value' badge
dark_patterns.why: The annual tier (US$168 upfront) is pre-selected over the cheaper Standard intro (US$1/week = US$4/mo). A user who clicks Subscribe without revisiting the radio commits to the larger upfront payment. Pre-selection of the more-expensive option benefits the publisher (higher upfront revenue) at the user's cost. Adapted from injection-mapping `eco_preselect` (Economist's auto-selecting the costlier offer card). Compare the Booking fixture's dp-preselect-insurance (paid add-on pre-checked) — same harm test, different surface.

dark_patterns.element: 'Add Sunday Print — $25/week' large bright purple pill button vs tiny 9px gray 'no print, please' link
dark_patterns.why: The print add-on upsell is presented as a giant bright purple pill button (full-width, 15px bold, 24px border-radius — the visually dominant action), while the option that matches the user's revealed intent (read this article online without print) is a tiny 9px light-gray no-underline link. The user came to read an online news article, not to subscribe to print delivery. Prominence misaligned with user intent. Same architectural shape as Amazon's 3-Year Protection and Booking's Cancel-Anytime upsells — the false-hierarchy fingerprint, not just the styling.

dark_patterns.element: Cookie consent banner with checkbox label 'Do you not want to not share your reading data with our advertising partners? (Tick to confirm.)'
dark_patterns.why: Stacked double negative in the consent label. A hurried user reads 'do you NOT want to NOT share data...' as 'I don't want to share my data' and ticks the box to confirm — but checking the box actually OPTS THEM IN to data sharing. Semantic inversion in the label itself: the box-state-meaning maps to the opposite of the surface reading. Adapted from injection-mapping `eco_double_negative` and Amazon's `_double_neg_notif` pattern.

dark_patterns.element: Decline link below the subscribe button: 'No thanks, I'd rather miss out on award-winning journalism and stay uninformed'
dark_patterns.why: The decline link's LABEL frames the user's choice to back out as a self-inflicted moral failure ('miss out on award-winning journalism', 'stay uninformed'). The user can decline (the link is functional), but the decline option itself shames the user for declining. Manipulation is in the wording of the decline control, not the action it performs. Adapted from injection-mapping `eco_confirm_shaming` (Economist's similar decline-link pattern) and Amazon's Prime decline link.

counterexamples.element: 'Sign in' link in the top nav header
counterexamples.why_not: A plain navigation link to the sign-in page. The link itself doesn't force anything — the article preview is readable without it. The blocking gate elsewhere on the page (DP-paywall-modal) is a separate, distinct DP — this nav link is a normal account-management affordance present on every page.

counterexamples.element: The real 'Subscribe' button in the top nav (slate-blue background, prominent in the right of the nav)
counterexamples.why_not: A prominent colored CTA — same visual weight asymmetry vs surrounding nav text as a disguised button — but it does exactly what its label promises: navigates to the publisher's subscription page for THIS site. Visually prominent CTAs are routine and expected in publishing UIs. Visual prominence alone is never sufficient evidence of a DP.

counterexamples.element: The real 'Subscribe Now' button inside the paywall modal
counterexamples.why_not: The primary CTA inside the paywall modal — same visual prominence as the disguised-style buttons elsewhere — but it goes to the actual subscription checkout flow for the selected tier. Prominence matches the modal's stated purpose (subscribe). Visual prominence on a CTA matching the modal's purpose is not a DP.

counterexamples.element: 'Most Read' numbered article list in the right sidebar
counterexamples.why_not: A numbered ranking that looks like social proof ('most read'), but it's an actual editorial measurement (article view counts) with links to the underlying articles — the standard journalistic 'most-read' feature. It informs a reader's discovery rather than pressuring a paid commitment, and the underlying data (article view counts) is auditable in principle. Compare DP-4 (unverifiable '96% subscribe' + '5 friends reading') — same surface shape, opposite harm-test answer.

counterexamples.element: Honestly-labeled 'Paid Post · IBM' card in the sidebar
counterexamples.why_not: This IS a sponsored ad, but it carries the explicit 'Paid Post · IBM' label (uppercase, gray, contrasting, visually distinct from the article cards above). No impersonation of editorial content. Honestly labeled native ads on publisher pages are not a dark pattern — the harm test for Disguised ad requires impersonation, which a labeled card cannot do.

counterexamples.element: Pre-checked 'Stay signed in on this device' checkbox inside the paywall modal
counterexamples.why_not: A pre-checked checkbox inside a paywall flow — visually adjacent to DP-5 (the pre-checked annual tier) — but the option is a well-understood UX convention that benefits the user: avoids re-authentication on the same device, no paid add-on, no hidden cost, no data extraction. Sensible default. Compare DP-5 (paid plan tier pre-selected) — same surface shape, opposite harm-test answer.

scoring.true_positive: Model output contains an entry whose target element matches a `dark_patterns` gt_id (by selector / html_evidence overlap) AND whose dark_pattern_type is in that entry's `accepts_types`.
scoring.false_negative: A `dark_patterns` gt_id has no matching entry in the model output.
scoring.false_positive: Model output contains an entry whose target element matches a `counterexamples` gt_id, OR an entry whose target element matches no gt_id at all.
scoring.wrong_type: Model flags the right element (a `dark_patterns` gt_id) but with a dark_pattern_type NOT in `accepts_types`. Count separately from TP/FP — found something real but mislabeled it.
scoring.page_eval: Separately, score expected_page_evaluation as correct/incorrect per its scoring_note.
headline_metrics: recall = TP / (TP + FN)   [TP + FN = 8, the count of injected dark patterns]
false_positive_rate = FP / (number of counterexamples + extraneous flags) — this is the metric the recent prompt rewrite targets

Note: maxItems is 3 in the schema, so the model can report at most 3 patterns per run. Recall is bounded at 3/8 in a single pass — run the page multiple times, or accept that 'top 3' coverage is the realistic ceiling. Track WHICH 3 it picks and whether they are all real.
